chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your need and the money closest to you

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How much money you need, and for what
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Calculate your total money need, your own contribution and the funding gap, by month.
This lesson builds toward: Given a farm plan with its costs, you will calculate the total money needed, your own contribution and the funding gap, split into working capital and equipment, with the month each is needed, with correct arithmetic and no household spending mixed in.
Before you look for money, write exactly what it is for. Working capital pays for one cycle of production: seed, fertilizer, feed, chicks or fingerlings, labour, vet services and transport. It comes back when you sell. Equipment and buildings (a pump, a pen, a store) last many years and pay back slowly. Lenders often treat them differently, with different loan lengths, so list them separately.
Example (made-up numbers in naira), a broiler batch in Nigeria: chicks, feed, vet services and labour 1,200,000 (working capital); drinkers, feeders and repairs to the house 300,000 (equipment). Total 1,500,000. You have saved 500,000. Funding gap = 1,500,000 - 500,000 = 1,000,000. That gap, not the total, is what you ask for.
Then put each cost in the month it is needed, using your cash-flow plan, so you can ask for money when you need it and not pay interest on money sitting idle. Keep a small buffer for price rises. Do not mix in household spending such as school fees: borrow for the farm only what the farm can repay.
Step by step:
- List every cost in your plan.
- Mark each one working capital or equipment.
- Add them up for the total need.
- Subtract the money you will put in yourself.
- The difference is your funding gap.
- Put each cost in the month it is needed, and add a small buffer.
Words to know:
- Working capital: money that pays for one cycle of production and comes back when you sell.
- Funding gap: the money you still need after your own contribution: total need - own money.
- Own contribution: the money or goods you put into the plan yourself.
Try it now: For one plan on your farm, list every cost, mark it working capital or equipment, add up the total, subtract your own money, and write the funding gap and the month each part is needed.
You can now work out exactly how much money your farm plan needs, what for and when, and the gap you need to fund.

check.q: A plan costs 800,000 and you have 300,000 of your own. What is the funding gap?
Which is working capital for a fish pond?
options: Fingerlings and feed for one cycle
check.why: Fingerlings and feed are used up in one cycle and come back when the fish are sold.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Savings groups, VSLAs and SACCOs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain how a VSLA and a SACCO work and list the rules to check before joining.
This lesson builds toward: Given a savings group, VSLA or SACCO you could join, you will explain how saving, borrowing, guarantees and share-out work in it and list its risks, naming at least three rules to check before you join.
A village savings and loan association (VSLA) is a group, often of 10 to 25 members, that meets every week. At each meeting members buy 1 to 5 shares at a share price the group fixes for the year. Savings go into a loan fund. Members can usually borrow up to three times their savings for up to three months, paying a service charge the group sets. Many groups also keep a small social fund for emergencies. After about a year, all loans are repaid and the money, including the service charges, is shared out in proportion to each member's savings.
A SACCO (savings and credit cooperative; in francophone West Africa, a mutuelle or caisse) is a member-owned financial cooperative, often larger and more formal. You save regularly, and loans are often linked to how much you have saved and need guarantors: members who promise to repay if you do not. In Kenya, SASRA licenses deposit-taking SACCOs and publishes the list. In the CFA franc countries, microfinance institutions and credit unions follow BCEAO rules.
Before you join, check: the written constitution or by-laws, the share price or savings amount, the loan rules and charges, how money is kept safe (a cash box with locks or a licensed account), how records are kept and read out, and what being a guarantor means. If you guarantee a friend's loan and they do not repay, you may have to pay.
Step by step:
- Ask to see the group's written rules.
- Check the share price or savings amount and meeting days.
- Check loan size, length and service charge.
- Check how cash and records are kept safe.
- Ask what being a guarantor means for you.
- For a SACCO, check it is registered or licensed.
Words to know:
- VSLA: village savings and loan association: a group that saves weekly, lends to members and shares out at the end of a cycle.
- Share-out: the day the group pays out all savings and earnings to members in proportion to their savings.
- SACCO: savings and credit cooperative: a member-owned group that takes savings and makes loans.
- Guarantor: a person who promises to repay a loan if the borrower does not.
Official sources:
- VSL Associates: the VSLA methodology (shares, loan fund, social fund, one-year cycle, share-out)
- SASRA, Kenya: list of licensed deposit-taking SACCOs
- BCEAO: rules for microfinance institutions (systemes financiers decentralises) in XOF countries
Try it now: Ask a savings group, VSLA or SACCO near you (or use the example) for its rules. Write the savings amount, loan size, loan length, charge, how cash is kept safe, and what a guarantor must do.
You can now explain how savings groups, VSLAs and SACCOs work and check their rules before you join or guarantee a loan.

check.q: In a VSLA, how is the money shared out at the end of the cycle?
options: In proportion to each member's savings
check.why: Members who bought more shares receive a bigger share of the total.

check.q: You guarantee a friend's SACCO loan and they stop paying. What may happen?
options: Nothing; guarantees are only a formality
You may have to repay part or all of it
check.why: A guarantor promises to repay if the borrower does not.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Microfinance and bank agricultural loans
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Compare two loan offers by total cost, collateral and how well repayments fit your harvest.
This lesson builds toward: Given two loan offers, you will compare their total cost, collateral and repayment dates and choose the one that fits your harvest, with the total repaid worked out for each and the repayment months checked against your cash flow.
Microfinance banks and institutions lend smaller amounts, often to groups; commercial and agricultural banks lend larger amounts, often against more security. Ask whether the rate is per month or per year, and whether it is flat or reducing balance. A flat rate charges interest on the full amount for the whole loan; a reducing-balance rate charges only on what you still owe, so the same number costs less. Add every fee and insurance charge to find the total you will repay.
Collateral is what the lender can take if you do not repay: a land title, a vehicle, equipment, savings held by the lender, a group guarantee, or a warehouse receipt. Some governments back lenders with credit guarantees, such as NIRSAL in Nigeria (up to 75% cover to lenders) and GIRSAL in Ghana. These protect the lender and can make banks more willing to lend to farmers, but you still owe the full loan.
Match repayments to your harvest. Example (made-up numbers in Kenya shillings), borrowing 100,000 for a maize season: Offer A is 10,000 a month for 12 months starting next month, a total of 120,000. Offer B is one payment of 112,000 in month 6, after harvest. B costs less and repays when your money comes in; A asks for repayments before you have sold anything. Ask for a grace period or harvest-time repayment, and check the lender is licensed by the central bank.
Step by step:
- Ask: rate per month or per year? Flat or reducing balance?
- Add interest, fees and insurance to get the total repaid.
- Ask what collateral or guarantee is needed.
- Put the repayment dates on your cash-flow plan.
- Ask for a grace period or harvest-time repayment if needed.
- Check the lender is licensed; read the contract fully.
Words to know:
- Flat rate: interest charged on the full amount borrowed for the whole loan, even as you repay.
- Reducing balance: interest charged only on the amount you still owe.
- Collateral: something the lender can take if you do not repay.
- Grace period: time at the start of a loan when you do not have to repay.
- Credit guarantee: a promise by a third party to cover part of the lender's loss if a borrower does not repay.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Nigeria: microfinance banks
- NIRSAL Plc, Nigeria: overview (credit risk guarantees for agricultural lending)
- Graphic Online, Ghana: GIRSAL honours financial institutions for agricultural lending
Try it now: Take two real or example loan offers. For each, write the amount, rate (per month or year, flat or reducing), fees, total repaid, collateral and repayment months. Mark the repayment months on your cash-flow plan and choose the one that fits better.
You can now compare loan offers by total cost, collateral and repayment timing and choose the one that fits your harvest.

check.q: Two loans show the same number, 2% a month. One is flat, one is reducing balance. Which usually costs less?
options: It depends on the colour of the form
check.why: Reducing balance charges only on what you still owe, so total interest is lower.

check.q: Your maize sells in month 6. Which repayment plan fits best?
options: A grace period with repayment after harvest
check.why: Repaying when your harvest money comes in avoids missed payments and forced sales.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Other doors to money, and asking for it

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Warehouse receipts and input credit
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the costs, duties and risks of a warehouse receipt loan and an input credit offer.
This lesson builds toward: Given a warehouse receipt or input credit offer, you will list its costs, what you must do and what happens if prices or the harvest fall, naming at least four terms and two risks.
Warehouse receipt financing: you deliver clean, dry, graded produce to a certified warehouse. It is weighed and tested, and you get a receipt that proves you own that amount and quality. A partner bank can lend against the receipt, so you get cash now and can sell later when prices may be better; the loan is repaid from the sale. In Kenya, the Warehouse Receipt System Council certifies warehouses. In Ghana, the Ghana Commodity Exchange and ARB Apex Bank launched electronic warehouse receipt loans in 2019, and in 2023 a savings and loans company joined to offer commodity-backed loans that farmers repay after they sell. Ask the lender how much of the produce's value it will lend and for how long.
Costs and risks: storage and handling fees, insurance, interest and transport. If prices fall instead of rising, the sale may not cover the loan and fees. Produce must meet the grade, so poor drying or sorting lowers its value. Work out the price you need with the storage break-even method from the risk management course.
Input credit: a buyer, processor, outgrower scheme or organisation supplies seed, fertilizer or chicks on credit, often with training, and you repay in instalments or the cost is taken from your harvest payment. One Acre Fund works this way with farmers in Kenya, Nigeria and other countries. Check: the input prices compared with cash prices, all charges, how much is deducted at harvest, whether you must sell only to them, what happens if the harvest fails, and the penalty for side-selling.
Step by step:
- Warehouse receipt: find a certified warehouse and its partner lenders.
- Ask the storage, handling, insurance and loan charges.
- Ask how much you can borrow against the produce and for how long.
- Work out the sale price you need to repay everything.
- Input credit: compare input prices with cash prices and list every charge.
- Ask what happens if the harvest fails and whether you must sell only to them.
Words to know:
- Warehouse receipt: a document from a certified warehouse proving you own stored produce of a set amount and quality.
- Certified warehouse: a store checked and approved to keep produce safely and issue receipts.
- Input credit: seed, fertilizer or other inputs supplied now and paid for later, often from the harvest.
- Outgrower scheme: an arrangement where a company supplies farmers with inputs and advice and buys their crop.
Official sources:
- Warehouse Receipt System Council, Kenya (certified warehouses and warehouse receipts)
- MyJoyOnline (31 October 2019): GCX and ARB Apex Bank launch electronic warehouse receipt financing
- Ghana News Agency (June 2023): Adehyeman Savings and Loans and Ghana Commodity Exchange partner to support farmers
- One Acre Fund: about us (financing, farm supplies and training; countries)
Try it now: Choose either a warehouse receipt loan or an input credit offer near you (or an example). Write at least four terms (costs, amount, length, deductions or selling rules) and two risks, and say whether it fits your farm.
You can now explain how warehouse receipt loans and input credit work and check their costs and risks before you sign.

check.q: What does a warehouse receipt prove?
options: That you own a set amount and quality of stored produce
That you have paid your taxes
That the bank has approved a loan
check.why: The receipt is proof of ownership of graded, stored produce, which a lender can accept.

check.q: An input credit scheme takes the input cost from your harvest payment. What must you check?
options: The input prices against cash prices, all charges and what happens if the harvest fails
Only the date of the training
check.why: These terms decide how much you really pay and who carries a crop failure.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Grants, youth programmes and avoiding scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a grant, youth programme or loan offer on an official source and spot the signs of a scam.
This lesson builds toward: Given a grant, youth programme or loan offer, you will check it on the official website or regulator list and spot the warning signs of a scam, before you pay, share details or apply.
Grants do not have to be repaid, but they are competitive, have rules on how you spend the money, and ask for reports. Many "youth funds" are really loans or training. Examples you can check: the African Development Bank's ENABLE Youth programme trains and supports young agripreneurs in several African countries, with partners such as IITA; Kenya's Youth Enterprise Development Fund offers loans to youth enterprises, including an Agri-Biz loan; Senegal's DER/FJ finances projects by women and young people, including in agriculture, mostly through credit. Programmes open and close and change their rules: always check on the official website or office that a call is open now before you apply.
Scams copy the names and logos of real programmes on social media and WhatsApp. Warning signs: you must pay a "processing" or "registration" fee before you get a grant or loan; approval is "guaranteed"; you are rushed; you are asked for your PIN, one-time code or ID photos by chat; the contact uses a personal number or email; or a loan app wants access to all your contacts. Real programmes do not charge to apply and never ask for your PIN.
Check every lender and loan app: in Kenya, the Central Bank of Kenya publishes the directory of licensed digital credit providers and SASRA lists licensed SACCOs; in Nigeria, the FCCPC publishes the register of approved digital lenders and the Central Bank of Nigeria licenses microfinance banks; in CFA franc countries, check with the BCEAO or the national microfinance office. If in doubt, ask your cooperative or extension officer.
Step by step:
- Find the programme on its official website or office, not a social media post.
- Check that the call is open now and read the rules.
- Never pay a fee to apply or to receive a grant.
- Never share your PIN, one-time code or passwords.
- Check lenders and loan apps on the regulator's list.
- Ask your cooperative or extension officer if unsure.
Words to know:
- Grant: money given for a purpose that does not have to be repaid, usually with rules and reports.
- Call for applications: a notice that a programme is accepting applications, with a start and end date.
- Scam: a trick to steal money or information.
- Regulator: the official body that licenses and supervises lenders, SACCOs or insurers.
Official sources:
- IITA: Sudan launches ENABLE Youth Program (African Development Bank youth agripreneur programme)
- Youth Enterprise Development Fund, Kenya (loans for youth enterprises, including an Agri-Biz loan)
- DER/FJ, Senegal: Delegation generale a l'Entrepreneuriat rapide des Femmes et des Jeunes
- Central Bank of Kenya: bank supervision, including the directory of licensed digital credit providers
- FCCPC, Nigeria: registration status of digital money lenders (approved loan apps)
Try it now: Find one grant, youth programme or loan app you have heard of. Check it on the official website or the regulator's list, and write: is it real, is it open now, is it a grant or a loan, and any warning signs you see.
You can now check whether a grant, programme or lender is real and open, and spot the warning signs of a scam.

check.q: A WhatsApp message says you have won a farm grant and must pay a 5,000 processing fee. What is this?
options: A warning sign of a scam
check.why: Real grants do not charge you to receive money.

check.q: In Nigeria, where can you check whether a loan app is approved?
options: The FCCPC register of digital lenders
check.why: The FCCPC publishes the list of approved digital money lenders.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a one-page funding request
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page funding request for your farm.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own farm figures, you will write a one-page funding request that a lender, programme or investor can assess, covering purpose, amount, own contribution, how it earns, repayment, collateral and risks.
A funding request tells a lender, programme or investor what you need, why, and how it will be repaid or pay off. Keep it to one page with clear headings: who you are and your farm (location, land, enterprises, years farming); the purpose and amount (total need, your own contribution, the gap you ask for, split into working capital and equipment); how it earns (cost per unit, gross margin or payback from your records); the finance you are asking for and why it fits; repayment plan by month, matched to your cash flow; collateral or guarantees; risks and how you manage them (insurance, contracts, diversification, storage); and your track record (records kept, past loans repaid, group membership).
Investors are different from lenders. An investor puts in money for a share of the business and its future profits (equity), instead of being repaid with interest. Equity investors usually look for growing businesses such as processors or larger farms with records and a team. You give up part of the ownership and some control, so get legal advice and never sign what you do not understand.
Before you send it, check the numbers twice, ask a cooperative leader, extension officer or adviser to read it, and attach your records. Never include passwords, PINs or full bank details in the request; give these only through the lender's official process.
Step by step:
- Who you are and your farm.
- Purpose, total need, own contribution and the gap.
- How it earns: cost per unit, margin or payback.
- Type of finance and repayment plan by month.
- Collateral or guarantees; risks and how you manage them.
- Track record; check the numbers and ask an adviser to read it.
Words to know:
- Funding request: a short document asking a lender, programme or investor for money, showing the purpose, amount and repayment.
- Equity: a share of ownership in a business that an investor gets for their money.
- Track record: proof of what you have done before, such as records kept and loans repaid.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page funding request with purpose, total need, own contribution and gap, how it earns, the type of finance and why, a monthly repayment plan, collateral, risks and your track record. Ask one person you trust to read it.
You can now write a clear one-page funding request backed by your own numbers that a lender, programme or investor can assess.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Need and funding gap The amount is a guess, or household spending is mixed in. Total need, own contribution and gap are correct, split into working capital and equipment, with months. Includes a small buffer and shows where each cost figure came from. Right kind of finance No reason is given for the type of finance chosen. Names the type of finance (group, SACCO, loan, warehouse receipt, input credit, grant or equity) and why it fits. Compares at least two options, including group savings, and explains the choice. Repayment plan No repayment plan, or repayments fall before any income. Monthly repayments with total cost, matched to the cash-flow plan and harvest. Shows what happens in a bad season and how repayments would still be met. Security and terms Collateral, guarantees or key terms are missing. Collateral or guarantees are named, with the main terms and two risks. Explains how a warehouse receipt, contract or insurance lowers the lender's risk. Checked and safe The lender or programme is not checked, or private details such as a PIN are included. The lender or programme is checked on an official site or regulator list, and no private codes are included. Notes the date checked and that the call or offer is open now. Clear one-page request Longer than one page or missing purpose, amount or how it earns. One page covering purpose, amount, own contribution, how it earns, repayment, collateral, risks and track record. Read by an adviser, with records attached and their comments addressed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the request and check it again.

check.q: Which amount should your request ask for?
options: The funding gap after your own contribution
The total cost, ignoring your own money
As much as the lender will give
Double the total cost to be safe
check.why: Asking for the gap shows your own commitment and keeps the loan as small as possible.

check.q: What does an equity investor get for their money?
options: A share of the business and its future profits
check.why: Equity means part ownership of the business.
